topic.title: Demonstration Learning and World Models for Robot Manipulation
topic.overview: Robot manipulation connects visual scene understanding with sequences of physical actions. These papers learn from demonstrations, pretrained visual features, and predictive world models, often decomposing long tasks into manageable stages. The challenge is to turn limited robot experience into policies that remain effective when objects, tasks, or embodiments change.
topic.whyItMatters: Demonstrations can reduce difficult exploration, while predictive models allow an agent to assess possible consequences. Their value depends on accurately representing contact and action effects, not simply producing visually plausible future frames.
topic.evolution: A 1995 example combines learned modules for gesture-guided pick-and-place. Later representatives study grasping and trajectory prediction. Recent work combines sequence imitation, reward learning, and large video-trained world models, broadening the available supervision beyond robot action labels without establishing a single inevitable development path.
openQuestions: When do human-video dynamics transfer to a robot’s actual action space?
How can long-horizon policies detect and recover from small execution errors?
